title: AST and ALT: Injury Pattern, Not Liver Function
bottomLine: AST and ALT primarily reflect hepatocellular injury, not hepatic synthetic function. Interpret the degree and pattern of elevation with symptoms, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, INR, albumin, medication/substance exposure and trend rather than calling any aminotransferase elevation 'liver failure'.
recognize: ALT is generally more liver-specific than AST; AST can also rise from skeletal muscle and other tissues.
Marked acute aminotransferase elevation raises concern for ischemic, toxic, viral or severe inflammatory hepatocellular injury, while mild chronic elevation has a broader differential.
differentiate: A hepatocellular pattern is dominated by aminotransferase elevation; a cholestatic pattern is dominated by alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin findings.
AST elevation with muscle injury should not automatically be labelled hepatic disease; clinical context and CK may clarify the source.
assessment: Assess abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, fever, hypotension, alcohol, acetaminophen and other medications/supplements, viral risk, pregnancy, metabolic risk and muscle symptoms.
Look for encephalopathy, bleeding, hypoglycemia or hemodynamic instability that would make liver injury an emergency.
workup: Trend AST/ALT with bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and synthetic-function markers; order cause-directed viral, autoimmune, metabolic, toxicology or imaging studies according to the pattern.
Avoid repetitive AST ordering when ALT and the clinical question already provide the relevant information unless a validated fibrosis score or specific hepatology question requires AST.
management: Treat the cause and remove hepatotoxic exposure when appropriate; urgent hospital/hepatology assessment is required when severe acute injury is accompanied by coagulopathy, encephalopathy, hypoglycemia or instability.
medicationSafety: Review acetaminophen dose/exposure, prescription drugs, herbal products and alcohol; medication-related injury can occur even when the drug was previously tolerated.
redFlags: Acute liver injury with rising INR
counselling: Explain that an abnormal enzyme is a clue to injury, not a diagnosis or direct measure of how well the liver is functioning.
followUp: Repeat testing based on severity, cause and trajectory; persistent unexplained elevation requires structured evaluation rather than indefinite serial panels.
examTrap: Calling elevated AST/ALT 'liver failure' while ignoring normal synthetic function—or assuming AST is hepatic when the patient has major muscle injury.
oneLinePearl: AST/ALT tell you about injury; INR, albumin and clinical status tell you more about function.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Clinical Biochemistry recommendations

title: Bilirubin and Jaundice: Fractionate the Problem
bottomLine: Jaundice is interpreted by bilirubin fraction, liver-enzyme pattern and clinical context. Predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia points toward overproduction or impaired conjugation; conjugated/direct hyperbilirubinemia raises hepatocellular or cholestatic disease and often changes the urgency of imaging or referral.
recognize: Dark urine is more consistent with conjugated bilirubin because unconjugated bilirubin is not water soluble.
Hemolysis, Gilbert syndrome and impaired conjugation can produce predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; obstruction and hepatocellular disease commonly increase conjugated bilirubin.
differentiate: Isolated bilirubin elevation with otherwise normal liver tests is different from jaundice plus cholestatic or hepatocellular enzyme abnormalities.
Neonatal jaundice has age-specific physiology and dangerous exceptions; adult bilirubin reasoning should not be copied onto newborns.
assessment: Assess stool/urine colour, pruritus, RUQ pain, fever, weight loss, medications, hemolysis symptoms, pregnancy and prior bilirubin pattern.
workup: Use total and direct/conjugated bilirubin with ALT/AST, alkaline phosphatase and cause-directed CBC/hemolysis studies or hepatobiliary imaging.
Do not order broader bile-acid testing as a substitute for the standard liver panel in a nonpregnant patient with suspected cholestasis unless a specific indication exists.
management: Urgently evaluate jaundice with fever/RUQ pain, sepsis, suspected obstruction, acute liver dysfunction or rapidly worsening bilirubin; otherwise manage the identified cause and follow the trend.
medicationSafety: Review drug-induced cholestasis/hepatitis risks and avoid adding potentially hepatotoxic medications before the cause is understood when clinically feasible.
redFlags: Pale stools/dark urine with obstruction concern
counselling: Explain that jaundice is a sign with multiple mechanisms and that bilirubin fraction helps determine where the problem is occurring.
followUp: Close the loop on imaging, hemolysis workup and repeat bilirubin when the cause is not immediately resolved.
examTrap: Treating every jaundiced patient as obstructed—or dismissing isolated unconjugated bilirubin elevation without checking the rest of the pattern.
oneLinePearl: First ask whether the bilirubin is conjugated or unconjugated; then interpret the rest of the liver pattern.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Biochemistry recommendations

title: Liver Function Patterns: Injury, Cholestasis, and Synthetic Failure
bottomLine: Interpret liver tests by pattern: hepatocellular injury, cholestasis and impaired synthetic function are related but not interchangeable. The dangerous patient is not necessarily the one with the highest ALT; worsening INR, encephalopathy, hypoglycemia or hemodynamic failure can signal true acute liver failure.
recognize: ALT/AST predominantly reflect injury, alkaline phosphatase plus bilirubin support a cholestatic pattern, and INR/albumin contribute information about synthetic function in the appropriate time frame.
Albumin changes slowly and is influenced by inflammation, nutrition, renal loss and other conditions, so a low value is not specific for acute hepatic failure.
differentiate: Acute severe hepatocellular injury can have very high aminotransferases before bilirubin rises substantially.
A falling AST/ALT is not automatically reassuring if the patient is clinically deteriorating and synthetic function is worsening.
assessment: Assess jaundice, encephalopathy, bleeding, volume status, ascites, infection, alcohol/medications, pregnancy and chronic liver disease history.
workup: Trend the relevant panel and use cause-directed ultrasound/vascular imaging, viral/toxicology/autoimmune testing or specialty evaluation based on the biochemical pattern and clinical syndrome.
management: Treat reversible causes, stop offending drugs when appropriate, manage complications and escalate suspected acute liver failure or biliary sepsis/obstruction urgently.
medicationSafety: Dose/avoid medications according to the actual hepatic condition and drug pharmacology; one abnormal enzyme does not justify blanket medication cessation.
redFlags: Rapid clinical deterioration despite falling enzymes
counselling: Explain that 'liver function tests' include markers of several different processes and are interpreted as a pattern, not a single pass/fail score.
followUp: Persistent abnormalities need a documented cause-directed plan, not indefinite repeat panels without a diagnostic question.
examTrap: Assuming improving AST/ALT means the liver is recovering while INR and mental status are worsening.
oneLinePearl: Enzymes show injury; the patient and synthetic markers show whether function is failing.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Clinical Biochemistry recommendations

title: CRP: Inflammation Marker, Not Infection Verdict
bottomLine: CRP is a nonspecific inflammatory marker. Use it to support a clinical question or trend response in selected conditions, not to diagnose bacterial infection, justify antibiotics or prove that inflammation has resolved in isolation.
recognize: CRP can rise with infection, inflammatory disease, tissue injury, malignancy and other physiologic stress.
A trend may be useful when the same clinical process is being followed, but kinetics must be interpreted with treatment timing and the patient's course.
differentiate: A high CRP does not distinguish bacterial infection reliably enough to replace history, examination, cultures or imaging.
A normal/low CRP does not exclude an early or localized serious illness when the clinical presentation is concerning.
assessment: Start with the syndrome: fever/source, inflammatory disease activity, postoperative course or other reason the test was ordered.
workup: Order or repeat CRP only when the result can reasonably change diagnosis, treatment or follow-up; avoid routine serial testing without a decision attached to it.
management: Treat the underlying syndrome, not the number; escalate based on organ dysfunction, hemodynamics and source-specific red flags.
medicationSafety: Do not prolong or broaden antibiotics solely because CRP remains elevated when the patient and microbiology support improvement.
redFlags: Clinical deterioration despite a reassuring CRP
Persistent unexplained systemic inflammation with weight loss or other alarm features
counselling: Explain that CRP tells us inflammation is present but usually cannot tell us exactly why.
followUp: Stop trending once the result no longer changes management.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because CRP is high without a compatible bacterial syndrome.
oneLinePearl: CRP answers 'is there inflammation?' far better than 'is this bacterial infection?'.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Labs Wisely

title: ESR: Slow, Nonspecific, Sometimes Useful
bottomLine: ESR is a slow, nonspecific marker influenced by age, anemia, pregnancy, proteins and chronic disease. It is useful for selected inflammatory questions and trends, but it should not be ordered as a universal screen for unexplained symptoms or interpreted as proof of one diagnosis.
recognize: ESR may be elevated in infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy and many noninflammatory states.
Because ESR changes more slowly than CRP, discordance between the two markers can occur and may be clinically explainable.
differentiate: An elevated ESR is not synonymous with polymyalgia rheumatica, giant-cell arteritis or infection.
A normal ESR does not absolutely exclude serious inflammatory disease when the clinical syndrome is compelling.
assessment: Tie the test to a specific question such as suspected inflammatory disease activity, giant-cell arteritis context or selected chronic infection evaluation.
workup: Interpret ESR with CBC, CRP and disease-specific tests only when they are clinically indicated; avoid broad inflammatory panels without a focused differential.
management: Treat the underlying diagnosis and use symptoms/function plus appropriate objective markers to follow response.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate corticosteroids or immunosuppression from an isolated ESR result without confirming the clinical disease context.
redFlags: Possible giant-cell arteritis with visual symptoms
Systemic illness/weight loss with unexplained marked inflammation
Clinical deterioration despite a normal marker
counselling: Explain that ESR is affected by many factors and is interpreted alongside the clinical picture.
followUp: Repeat only when the trend is expected to influence a known disease-management decision.
examTrap: Diagnosing an inflammatory disorder from an elevated ESR alone.
oneLinePearl: ESR is a context test, not a diagnosis machine.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Labs Wisely

title: Procalcitonin: Stewardship Adjunct, Not a Sepsis Gatekeeper
bottomLine: Procalcitonin can support antimicrobial-stewardship decisions in selected settings, especially when interpreted serially with a validated protocol, but it must not delay empiric treatment of a clinically unstable patient or be used alone to diagnose or exclude bacterial infection.
recognize: Bacterial infection can raise procalcitonin, but levels are affected by timing, severity, renal dysfunction and noninfectious systemic inflammation.
The value is most useful when the clinical pathway already defines how it will change an antibiotic decision.
differentiate: A low result early in infection does not safely rule out sepsis in a deteriorating patient.
A high result does not identify the source or organism and does not replace cultures/source evaluation.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, organ dysfunction, likely source, immune status, recent surgery/trauma and antibiotic exposure before interpreting the number.
workup: Use cultures, imaging and source-specific diagnostics according to the syndrome; if procalcitonin is used, follow the validated local protocol rather than an improvised universal threshold.
management: Start time-sensitive antibiotics when severe bacterial infection/sepsis is clinically likely; use biomarker trends only as adjunctive evidence for stewardship/de-escalation when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not withhold antibiotics from septic shock because procalcitonin is low, and do not prolong broad therapy solely because it remains elevated.
counselling: Explain that the test estimates part of the inflammatory response and cannot by itself prove whether an infection is bacterial.
followUp: Stop serial testing when it no longer changes stewardship or clinical management.
examTrap: Waiting for procalcitonin before treating a patient with clear sepsis physiology.
oneLinePearl: Procalcitonin can refine antibiotic decisions; it cannot overrule a crashing patient.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Thyroid Function Tests: Know When TSH Can Be Trusted
bottomLine: TSH is the principal first-line test for most suspected primary thyroid disease when the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is intact. Free T4 becomes essential when TSH is abnormal, central disease is suspected, pregnancy/severe illness changes interpretation, or treatment monitoring requires it.
recognize: High TSH with low free T4 supports primary hypothyroidism; suppressed TSH with elevated free hormone supports primary hyperthyroidism.
Central hypothyroidism can present with low free T4 and an inappropriately normal or low TSH, so a 'normal' TSH can be misleading.
differentiate: Acute severe illness and assay interference can distort thyroid tests; abnormal results during illness do not automatically equal primary thyroid disease.
Biotin and some medications can interfere with assays or thyroid physiology and should be considered when results do not fit the patient.
assessment: Assess symptoms, pregnancy, pituitary symptoms, amiodarone/lithium exposure, thyroid medication timing/adherence, supplements and recent severe illness.
workup: Use TSH first for most primary-thyroid questions, adding free T4 when indicated; avoid routine free T3/free T4/antibody panels without a clinical question.
management: Treat the confirmed disorder and monitor with the test appropriate to the physiology; in central disease, TSH should not be the sole dosing target.
medicationSafety: Do not change levothyroxine repeatedly before steady-state reassessment unless the clinical situation requires earlier action; review absorption interactions such as iron/calcium.
counselling: Explain why one thyroid number is not always enough and why timing/adherence can alter results.
followUp: Repeat after a clinically appropriate interval for dose changes and sooner when pregnancy or severe disease requires closer monitoring.
examTrap: Ruling out hypothyroidism because TSH is normal in a patient with low free T4 and pituitary disease symptoms.
oneLinePearl: TSH is powerful when the pituitary axis is trustworthy; free T4 rescues the cases where it is not.
sourceBasis: BC Guidelines: Thyroid Function Testing in the Diagnosis and Monitoring of Thyroid Function Disorder

title: Glucose Interpretation: Acute Value, Chronic Diagnosis, or Treatment Effect?
bottomLine: Interpret glucose by timing, symptoms and context. A fasting, random or post-load glucose can diagnose diabetes only when the applicable Canadian criteria are met; acute illness, medications, pregnancy and hypoglycemia require different decisions than routine chronic screening.
recognize: Diabetes Canada diagnostic glucose thresholds differ by fasting, 2-hour OGTT and random symptomatic testing.
Stress hyperglycemia can occur during acute illness and still predicts future diabetes risk, but one inpatient high value does not automatically establish chronic type 2 diabetes.
differentiate: Symptomatic diagnostic-range hyperglycemia can establish diabetes without waiting for a second test; an asymptomatic abnormal result generally requires confirmation according to the diagnostic pathway.
Hypoglycemia is an immediate safety problem regardless of whether the patient meets chronic diabetes criteria.
assessment: Clarify fasting/meal timing, symptoms, diabetes/pregnancy history, insulin or secretagogue use, steroids/acute illness, renal function and recent nutrition/exercise.
workup: Use A1C, repeat fasting glucose or OGTT when appropriate for chronic diagnosis; assess ketones/electrolytes/acid-base status urgently when DKA/HHS is possible.
management: Treat severe hypo- or hyperglycemic emergencies first; for stable dysglycemia, confirm/classify the disorder and select treatment by comorbidity, hypoglycemia risk and patient goals.
medicationSafety: Insulin and insulin secretagogues can produce dangerous hypoglycemia; SGLT2 inhibitors can be associated with ketoacidosis even without extreme hyperglycemia.
counselling: Explain whether the value reflects screening, diagnosis, treatment monitoring or an acute emergency; those are different clinical questions.
followUp: Close the loop on confirmatory testing after stress hyperglycemia or an asymptomatic diagnostic-range result.
examTrap: Calling one stress-related inpatient glucose elevation chronic type 2 diabetes—or delaying emergency treatment because diagnostic confirmation is incomplete.
oneLinePearl: A glucose number only makes sense after you know when it was drawn and why.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Definition, Classification and Diagnosis guidance
